cultivar: Pingyang local landrace (Pingyang Tezao) and Fuding Dabai
processing: A bud with one or two leaves is pan-fired, lightly rolled, then put through repeated cycles of piling to yellow and gentle baking (the local description is 'nine yellowings and nine bakings'), which turns dry leaf, liquor and wet leaf all yellow.
harvest_season: Spring, from late March to mid April; pre-Qingming and yu qian lots.
appearance_dry: Fine, slightly curled shoots in a distinct yellow-green with golden tips and soft down.
appearance_liquor: Bright clear yellow, deeper than other yellow teas.
appearance_wet: Even, tender bud-and-leaf sets in a true pale yellow.
taste_profile: Mellow and sweet with cooked chestnut, sweet corn and a faint floral note, thick for a bud tea and entirely without harshness.

brewing.notes: Gaiwan or glass at 85 °C. More thorough yellowing than most, so it takes slightly hotter water and gives a steady four steeps.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring harvest in pre-Qingming and yu qian lots, in small quantities and mostly within Zhejiang; the style is said to have nearly disappeared in the twentieth century, and production is still limited. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Pingyang Huang Tang, 'yellow soup of Pingyang', is the best-known yellow tea of southern Zhejiang, from the hills of Pingyang county south of Wenzhou and neighbouring counties. The name is literal: the liquor is a proper clear yellow, deeper than most yellow teas, because the yellowing here is unusually thorough. It is also a survivor; the method is said to have nearly died out in the twentieth century before being revived.

After pan-firing and a light roll, the leaf goes through repeated cycles of piling, during which it warms and yellows, and gentle baking to halt the process, the local shorthand being 'nine yellowings and nine bakings'. The aim is the 'three yellows': yellow dry leaf, yellow liquor, yellow wet leaf. It takes days and a lot of judgement, and it is why the tea is scarce.

In the cup it is mellow and sweet, cooked chestnut and sweet corn with a faint floral lift, thicker than most bud teas and completely without the grassy or astringent edge of a green. Because the yellowing is so complete it takes slightly hotter water than a green, 85 °C, and gives a steady four steeps in a gaiwan. It is a tea for people who find bud teas thin.

It is sold as the spring harvest of the current year in pre-Qingming and yu qian lots, almost all of it within Zhejiang, where it has a loyal Wenzhou following. The checks are the colour, which should be genuinely yellow in leaf and cup rather than green, and the picking date. A green-looking 'Huang Tang' has been rushed.

It is the best yellow tea to show someone what the category is about, precisely because the yellowing is not shy.
history:
Pingyang Huang Tang is a strip-shaped yellow tea from southern Zhejiang, usually credited with a little over 200 years of history. Despite the county in its name it is not confined to Pingyang: Taishun, Rui'an and Yongjia make it too, which is why it is also called Wenzhou Huang Tang.

The traditional description of the leaf is 'white heart, yellow leaf', yellow overall with the white down showing. Beyond that little is documented in detail about who made it known or how the method changed, and the accounts of its decline and revival in the twentieth century are hard to date.
